theme: Doctrinal Pause: Regeneration and the New Birth
summary: The Spirit’s sovereign work of giving new life; the necessity and nature of being born again
readingInstruction: Read John 3:1-21, Ezekiel 36:25-27, and Titus 3:3-7. Today is a doctrinal pause on regeneration, the new birth. Notice who does the work in each passage.
settingTheScene: Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born again. Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, was confused, and Jesus replied that he should have understood. The promise of a new heart is found in the prophets, especially Ezekiel. In Titus, Paul speaks of the same event in the life of the believer: the washing of regeneration. The doctrine of regeneration is the teaching that God, by his Spirit, gives new spiritual life to those who were dead in sin.
observation: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3).
“Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).
“That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).
“I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses” (Ezekiel 36:25).
“And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
“And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).
“And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).
“He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).
doctrinalFocus: Regeneration is the act of God by which he gives new spiritual life to a person who was dead in sin. It is the beginning of the Christian life. Jesus calls it being born again or born from above. The Bible teaches that we are born spiritually dead (Ephesians 2:1) and cannot save ourselves. God makes us alive. In the language of Ezekiel, he replaces a heart of stone with a heart of flesh and puts his Spirit within us. As in physical birth, the one being born does not bring about the birth: it is a work of God, “not of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13). Reformed Christians have generally taught that regeneration comes first in order and produces the faith and repentance by which we respond to the gospel. Other evangelicals place regeneration and faith more closely together, but all agree that salvation is the Spirit’s gift and that those who are born again will show it in a new love for God, new obedience, and perseverance. It is not something we achieve. It is something we receive.
interpretation:
Jesus’ words to Nicodemus show how radical the need is. A morally serious, religious man needs not improvement but new birth. “That which is born of the flesh is flesh.” Human nature cannot produce spiritual life. Only “that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.” Then Jesus compares the Spirit to the wind. You cannot control it, and you cannot predict it, but you can see its effects. The new birth is God’s sovereign work.

The Old Testament had promised it. Ezekiel 36 speaks of a day when God would gather his people, cleanse them with water, give them a new heart, and put his Spirit within them so that they would walk in his ways. This is the new covenant promise, along with Jeremiah 31. When Jesus mentions water and the Spirit, Nicodemus should have thought of this passage. The problem under the old covenant was a heart of stone, a will that would not obey. The solution is not better instruction but a new heart.

Paul says the same in Titus 3. He describes our past: foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to passions, hated and hating. Then “the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared.” He saved us not because of works but according to his own mercy, “by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior.” Regeneration is purely a gift, and the result is that we become heirs with the hope of eternal life.

The doctrine comforts and humbles. It humbles because we contributed nothing to our new life. It comforts because the one who began it will finish it. And it presses us to look for the signs of life in ourselves, such as love for Christ, hatred of sin, and a desire to obey, and to pray for those who are dead in sin that God would make them alive.
connection: Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 11:19-20 also promise a new heart. Deuteronomy 30:6 speaks of the circumcision of the heart. Ephesians 2:1-5 says we were dead in trespasses and God made us alive with Christ. 1 Peter 1:3 and 1:23 speak of being born again. 2 Corinthians 5:17 says anyone in Christ is a new creation. John 1:12-13 says we are born of God. 1 John 3:9 and 5:1 describe those who are born of God.
application:
Look for evidence of the Spirit’s work in you: love for God, sorrow for sin, hunger for the Word. Thank God for each.

Pray by name for someone who seems far from God. Ask God to give them a new heart.

Read Ezekiel 36:25-27 as a prayer, in the first person: “Give me a new heart and put your Spirit in me.”
prayerPrompts: Thank God for making you alive when you were dead in sin.
Thank him for the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Spirit.
Ask him to show you where new life is evident in you.
